title: Inversión extranjera directa en México alcanza récord de 43 mil millones de dólares de enero a septiembre
rawText:
La Inversión Extranjera Directa (IED) en México alcanzó un máximo histórico de 43 mil 90 millones de dólares (mdd) durante los primeros nueve meses de este año, un crecimiento anual de 5.3 por ciento, informó la Secretaría de Economía.
La cifra representa la mayor captación de inversión extranjera para un periodo de enero a septiembre desde que se tiene registro, de acuerdo con el reporte de la dependencia, que destacó el crecimiento sostenido de los flujos de capital hacia el país desde 2021.
El avance estuvo impulsado principalmente por la industria manufacturera, que recibió 19 mil 231 mdd, equivalente a 44.6 por ciento de la IED total y un incremento anual de 26.6 por ciento. Le siguieron los servicios financieros y de seguros, con 10 mil 635 mdd, y transportes, correos y almacenamiento, con 3 mil 99 mdd.
Por tipo de inversión, la reinversión de utilidades concentró la mayor parte de los recursos, con 34 mil 975 mdd, equivalentes a 81.2 por ciento del total y el monto más elevado desde que se tiene registro. Este componente aumentó 26 por ciento anual. En contraste, las nuevas inversiones sumaron 3 mil 800 mdd, 8.8 por ciento del total, mientras que las cuentas entre compañías alcanzaron 4 mil 315 mdd, equivalentes a 10 por ciento.
En cuanto al origen de los capitales, Estados Unidos se mantuvo como el principal inversionista en México, con 19 mil 334 mdd, 44.9 por ciento del total.
Miguel González Ibarra, catedrático de la Facultad de Economía de la UNAM, explicó que las compañías siguen a la espera de que se aclaren las oportunidades de negocio, particularmente ante la revisión del T-MEC y los problemas de seguridad interna, especialmente en el transporte de mercancías, un factor que puede elevar los costos y riesgos de operar en México.
“El país necesita adoptar una estrategia más proactiva para atraer nuevos proyectos, en lugar de depender de las decisiones de expansión de las empresas que ya tienen presencia en territorio nacional”.
Por su parte, Alejandro H. Garza Salazar, director de inversiones y fundador de Aztlan Equity Management, consideró que la elevada reinversión de utilidades refleja que las empresas multinacionales que ya operan en México continúan encontrando oportunidades de rentabilidad y expansión en el mediano y largo plazos.
No obstante, señaló que el comportamiento de los flujos también evidencia una transición en el nearshoring, ya que el crecimiento de la inversión depende cada vez más de compañías que ya cuentan con instalaciones en el país y amplían su capacidad productiva, en lugar de la llegada de nuevos participantes.
Buen panorama para la inversión en México
Janneth Quiroz, directora de análisis económico de Monex, afirmó que la inversión local ha registrado un comportamiento más moderado por la incertidumbre de reformas internas; sin embargo, el país tiene un buen panorama a nivel global por la buena relación con EU.
“Desde afuera, aplauden la relación entre Sheinbaum y Trump. La perspectiva es que se ha hecho un buen manejo de esta política diplomática entre los dos países. Hasta podríamos decir que es de sus ‘consentidas’”, indicó.
En conferencia, argumentó que los inversionistas globales han decidido apostar por el país a pesar de la incertidumbre comercial, ya que existen amplias oportunidades con el boom de la inteligencia artificial.

title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
rawText:
Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.
Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.
Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.
"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.
The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.
Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."
Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.
"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."
Morocco raises concerns over CAS process
Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.
In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.
The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.
Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."
CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.
Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.
Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."
Trouble on the field and in the stands
Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.
The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).
Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.
Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.
The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead

title: "Le digo a mi hijo que son solo fuegos artificiales": cómo es vivir en una ciudad de Yemen sitiada por los rebeldes hutíes
rawText:
"Le digo a mi hijo que son solo fuegos artificiales": cómo es vivir en una ciudad de Yemen sitiada por los rebeldes hutíes
  - Autor, Orla Guerin*
  - Título del autor, Corresponsal internacional sénior de la BBC
  - Informa desde, Estanbul
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 10 min
En la ciudad yemení de Taiz, rodeada de montañas escarpadas y combatientes rebeldes hutíes, Ashwaq solo tiene una manera de intentar calmar a su asustado hijo: mentir.
"Cuando mi hijo de 11 años oye un ruido fuerte, le digo: "No tengas miedo, son solo fuegos artificiales"", cuenta.
"No quiero que se asuste, pero en el fondo sé que tiene edad suficiente para comprender lo que sucede a su alrededor. Ha vivido la guerra durante la mayor parte de su vida".
Taiz ha sido durante mucho tiempo un objetivo estratégico, y una línea de frente, en la guerra civil de Yemen.
Las fuerzas hutíes reforzaron su cerco el mes pasado, rodeando por completo la ciudad controlada por el gobierno y a su población, estimada entre 600.000 y un millón de habitantes.
Desde entonces, la tercera ciudad más grande de Yemen ha estado aislada del mundo y las voces de sus habitantes apenas se han escuchado. Contactamos con siete personas dentro de la ciudad que nos explicaron la magnitud del asedio.
Ofrecieron relatos detallados del férreo control que los hutíes ejercen sobre Taiz. Apenas puede entrar una cantidad mínima de alimentos.
Los precios de productos básicos como el arroz, el azúcar y el aceite de cocina se han duplicado o incluso triplicado.
Los suministros esenciales, como medicinas, agua y combustible, escasean.
Fin de Anuncio app
En las calles que antes bullían con el tráfico y el murmullo constante, reina el silencio. Las escuelas y los restaurantes están cerrados. El sufrimiento se agrava.
Montones de basura se acumulan en la ciudad, junto a la gente. Cuando los residentes intentan deshacerse de ella quemándola, se genera un humo tóxico. Incluso el aire se ha convertido en un arma para los hutíes.
Desde posiciones en las colinas, los combatientes rebeldes —y los francotiradores— pueden librar una guerra contra la ciudad que se extiende a sus pies.
Las estimaciones sobre el número de muertos varían mucho. En la Oficina de Asuntos de Asedio, un departamento del gobierno local, afirman que 148 civiles han muerto en los ataques de los hutíes desde agosto.
Algunas de las personas con las que contactamos en Taiz prefieren permanecer en el anonimato por temor a su seguridad.
Muchos en la ciudad se muestran reacios incluso a hablar por teléfono, ya que los hutíes controlan las principales compañías de telefonía móvil.
"A veces siento que la ciudad se ha convertido en una enorme prisión", dice Ashwaq, maestra y madre de tres hijos, quien prefirió que solo se usara su nombre de pila. Añora el antiguo Taiz.
"Antes era una ciudad vibrante", dice. "La gente amaba la vida, trabajaba duro, se visitaba y tenía esperanzas en el futuro, a pesar de todas las dificultades. Ahora, casi no salimos. Los bombardeos [de los hutíes] pueden ocurrir en cualquier momento, y los francotiradores cerca del frente hacen que incluso un viaje corto sea peligroso".
Ella mantiene a su hijo y a sus dos hijas mayores dentro de casa.
"Me preocupo por ellos todos los días, a todas horas y, sinceramente, a todos los minutos", dice.
Una ciudad estratégica
La guerra no es algo nuevo para Taiz. Esta ciudad estratégica es la puerta de entrada a Adén, sede provisional del gobierno reconocido internacionalmente, así como también al sur de Yemen.
Los rebeldes hutíes, respaldados por Irán, llegaron a las afueras de Taiz en 2015, cortando las carreteras y sitiando la ciudad desde tres flancos. Un año antes, habían tomado la capital de Yemen, Saná.
Más de una década después, el gobierno, débil y fragmentado, no ha logrado recuperar la capital ni gran parte del noroeste de Yemen. Esto a pesar del apoyo de Arabia Saudita y sus ataques aéreos.
En los últimos meses, el conflicto se ha recrudecido y se ha expandido

title: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
rawText:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around.
No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world.
According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source.
Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”
Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee.
Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled.
The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”

title: Officials Brief Congressional Staff on Intelligence Surrounding Nvidia Affair
rawText: After President Trump said Jensen Huang was not a security threat, U.S. intelligence agencies told aides to lawmakers there was no evidence the woman at the heart of the scandal took directions from the Chinese spy agency.

title: Trump says pardon is always an option for Huang, and that invoking the Fifth isn’t necessary
rawText:
President Donald Trump said that while pardoning Jensen Huang for any potential criminal activity remains an option, he doesn’t think that will be needed for the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO.
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” Trump told the New York Post in an interview published Tuesday night.
Asked about Huang’s scheduled appearances next week on Capitol Hill, Trump said, “I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people.”
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person,” the president said.
A representative for Huang declined to comment on Trump’s comments. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
Speaking at a news conference Tuesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated he would have told Trump if Huang had been involved in any criminal activity.
“To the extent that, that the department, that the Department of Justice had information that he was committing crimes or something like this, that is, that is, that’s just not, that’s something that I would have certainly told the president had it been true,” Blanche said.
In Congress, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are preparing to grill Huang over their national security concerns.

Huang, who has not been charged with a crime, resigned from his post as CEO of the chip giant following reports that he had a relationship with a woman who U.S. intelligence agencies believed was a Chinese spy. In a Nov. 8 memo to Nvidia’s staff, he said, “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Trump worked behind the scenes over the weekend to get Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back. That move has been met with bipartisan backlash.
Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., on Monday raised concerns over Nvidia’s quick reversal to rehire Huang after indicating it wouldn’t.
“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” Ricketts wrote in a post on X.
Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., wrote that with Nvidia’s rehiring of Huang, “the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens.”
Cramer and Ricketts are both members of the Senate Banking Committee, where Huang is scheduled to testify in public Dec. 3.
In celebrating Huang’s return, Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social post that the U.S. government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Similarly, Nvidia’s board said it reached the decision to reinstate Huang after receiving “input from senior levels of the United States government” that his “reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
rawText:
A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, according to reports from NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile, Cisco, and Motorola.
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
The Chinese telecom giant was also found guilty of bank fraud.
The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng, whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement. The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns.
In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit.” Huawei plans to appeal the decision and may face fines, forfeiture, and restitution, according to Bloomberg.
Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

title: Pochettino leads Man Utd fury at Yoro red card ruling
rawText:
Pochettino leads Man Utd fury at Yoro red card ruling
- Published
Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has questioned the competence of video assistant referee officials after defender Leny Yoro had his red card overturned by the Football Association.
Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday after bringing down Aleksander Isak just outside the United penalty area.
United sources say they have conclusive proof it was impossible for Isak to reach the ball after he took a heavy touch, that it would have run on to goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Yoro should not have been punished for denying a goalscoring opportunity.
Pochettino said he had some sympathy with referee Sam Barrott but he is livid at how the situation played out.
"I am very disappointed," the Argentine said. "This type of thing can never happen.
"We can accept the referee can make a mistake. But if we have VAR, what were they doing? What were they doing? Are we going to repeat the game? Are we going to have the possibility to play 11 by 11? No.
"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be at the level to drive [it]. We accept that the technology is there but what are they doing?"
United are furious at both the nature of the audio of the incident, and referees' chief Howard Webb defending referee Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' reinforcing it on the Mic'd Up programme, which was shown on Sky Sports.
They intend to take the matter up with both the Premier League and ProRef.
It is the second time this season United been on the wrong end of a major VAR error.
Webb apologised to United after Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford on 13 September was allowed to stand even though a clearly offside Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play.
There has been no apology from Webb on this occasion.
Instead, he has doubled down on the call, saying: "I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball."
United sources claim this interpretation is wrong.
The club are unhappy at the speed the on-field decision was confirmed. It is thought United used data around Isak's top speed and his chances of reaching the ball in their defence of Yoro to the FA. They claim this could have been done "within minutes" of the incident occurring.
This is not the only bone of contention at Old Trafford around the incident.
Pochettino also pointed out Liverpool forward Bradley Barcola was too close to the United wall from the resulting free-kick and Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal should have been disallowed.
"No-one talked about [the fact] that the goal wasn't legal," said Pochettino. "Barcola was touching our wall. It must be disallowed.
"We need to defend my players and my club, and that is to denounce it and to say, the decision wasn't good. And now, the three points, where are the three points?"
Webb defends Yoro red card
What referee's chief Webb said about the incident on the Mic'd Up programme.
"There's a question mark, I guess, around whether or not he would get onto that ball before Lammens. Now, in the moment, the referee looked at it and felt he would.
"That was the referee's call made on the field, and then the VAR checks that to see whether that decision made on the field was clearly and obviously incorrect, and formed the opinion that it wasn't.
"That if there was any doubt, then it was doubt.
"It wasn't going to be something that was clearly and obviously wrong and therefore allowed that decisive on-field decision to stand. and
"I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball.
"The alternative view is that Lammens might get there first, but I think it's a little bit debatable. Certainly not clearly wrong."

title: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
rawText:
After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.
Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”
The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.
The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.
The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The President reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role
Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes.
Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of Congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

title: GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
rawText:
Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.
GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.
Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI.”
PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.
At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

title: How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
rawText:
How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
Loading...
As Sean Gilbert stepped out of his white GMC pickup, he breathed in the scent of applewood and Columbia Basin dust. Here, just south of Wapato, Wash., one of his 50-acre Gala and Red Delicious apple orchards is ground into huge piles of mulch chips. The wood chipper is the size of a semi-truck and belts out a screeching racket.
He said this ground will lay fallow. It will cost this fifth-generation apple farmer less to leave it unplanted and weedy than to plant another orchard or crop. He scooped up a handful of applewood mulch. "It's a bit of a relief that we're not going to continue to be hemorrhaging dollars on orchards that the market doesn't want," he said. "It hasn't been making sense for a while."
Washington's $9 billion industry grows nearly 70% of the nation's fresh apples, according to Jon DeVaney, president of the Washington State Tree Fruit Association.
DeVaney said farmers are being pressed by the costs of labor, fuel, fertilizer, equipment, as well as weak exports from international tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.
He estimated thousands of acres of apple orchards across the Northwest are being rapidly torn out, or are not being actively cared for, because many farmers aren't making money growing the fruit. And after several years of similar economic conditions, many farms have gone deep into debt – with even some large, well-established operations filing for bankruptcy.
Loading...
In the late summer and fall, unpicked apples have been left to rot in branches and on the ground. Over the past few years, an estimated thousands of acres have only been partially picked or not picked at all, according to Kate Tynan, senior vice president of the Northwest Horticultural Council, a trade association that advocates for the Northwest tree fruit industry on federal policy issues and international trade.
Recent federal regulatory changes would effectively lower wages for some immigrant workers and take housing costs out of their paychecks. Tynan said with updates to the way wages are calculated, farm owners are hoping they'll be able to break even – but the farm workers union has pushed back on these changes and an upcoming federal judicial decision could put operators on the hook for backpay for the 2026 season.
U.S. farmers have also been especially hard hit by tariffs and high input costs. The Trump administration announced $12 billion in payments to farmers at the end of 2025 that primarily targeted farmers who grow crops such as soybeans and corn. Tynan said much of that relief has not reached farmers that grow specialty crops like fruit and vegetables.
"The Pacific Northwest has lost an unprecedented number of tree fruit farms in recent years," Tynan said. "Economic conditions have worsened drastically since then, so we know that number is far higher today."
She points to a USDA census conducted every five years that recorded a 15% drop in Washington tree fruit farms between 2017 and 2022. In neighboring Oregon, more than a quarter of apple, pear and cherry farms were lost in that same time period. By the numbers, apple acreage in Washington increased slightly during this period. But small, family-run farms face another threat: large, well-funded corporations are buying out orchard owners, reducing competition when profits are already tight.
"Some of that was new investment from [private equity] coming in during that time. That acreage trend has since reversed," said Jon DeVaney, emphasizing that the industry is losing growers.
"From 2023, 2024 and 2025 have been the really hard years," said Sean Gilbert, who co-owns Gilbert Orchards, a family-run company founded in 1898 that manages 4,000 acres of fruit in Washington state.

title: El papa Francisco revela en su diario que vio al diablo 3 veces, así como "las puertas del infierno"
rawText:
El papa Francisco revela en su diario que vio al diablo 3 veces, así como "las puertas del infierno"
  - Autor, Redacción BBC Mundo *
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 4 min
En nuevos extractos de su diario privado, el difunto papa Francisco afirma haber visto al diablo tres veces a lo largo de su vida.
En el libro "Diario privado del papa Francisco", publicado este martes, también se exponen fragmentos personales del Papa en los que revela parte de sus preocupaciones, arrepentimientos y autocríticas.
Unos de los más llamativos son en los que él describe tres encuentros con el diablo.
El primero fue desde un coche, otro "en el coro" durante una misa y un tercero durante una reunión con funcionarios del Vaticano.
"No puedo olvidar el potente tono ronco de su voz", escribió Francisco, recordando una de las visiones. Dijo que no podía olvidar sus ojos "amenazantes".
"Me miró con ojos llameantes... Eran como destellos de fuego", escribió sobre su segunda visión, que según él ocurrió dentro de una capilla carmelita mientras era arzobispo de Buenos Aires.
Dijo que la presencia del diablo se entrometía en sus viajes, incluso durante su visita a Chile en medio del escándalo de abusos sexuales por parte del clero, y en una reunión pocos días después de su regreso a Roma.
"Lo vi y oí su voz, triunfante, poseyéndolo todo", escribió, y añadió que "el Señor me dio la oportunidad de liberarme de estos encuentros".
El difunto papa, quien dirigió la Iglesia católica durante 12 años hasta su muerte en 2025, también reveló que mientras se preparaba para irse a dormir en junio de 2018, "vio las puertas del infierno".
En sus escritos personales, expresó: "Vi un poco y me aterrorizó". Incluso tomó el rosario como un arma.
"Es peligroso acercarse a las puertas del infierno, porque pueden surgir llamas que queman".
Arrepentimiento tras su visita a Chile
Fin de Anuncio app
En su diario íntimo, también expresa su arrepentimiento por su visita a Chile en 2018, cuando fue criticado por defender a un obispo acusado de encubrir abusos sexuales cometidos por un sacerdote.
Posteriormente pidió disculpas y convocó a los obispos del país a Roma, donde todos ofrecieron su renuncia.
En una entrada de 2021 escribió haber quedado "devastado por la situación en Chile".
"Me costó mucho aceptar lo que pasó en Chile; no pensé que fuera tan grave".
Según la agencia AFP, Francisco se critica en varias ocasiones a lo largo del texto, ya sea por sus "sentimientos de desprecio, envidia y orgullo" o por haber ignorado a un hombre ebrio que le habló en la calle porque "quería dar un paseo tranquilo".
El 15 de enero de 2017 confesó que llevaba varios días experimentando "un espíritu muy malo de ira y descontento".
Francisco sufrió una crisis espiritual durante dos años, a partir de 2021. En ese momento, se refirió a su lucha contra el deseo de ser alguien que "utilizara a los demás como marionetas".
"Todo se mezclaba con problemas de gobernanza, presión en cuanto a las decisiones que había que tomar, aridez y desolación", escribió en una entrada de diciembre de 2022.
Su diario personal al mundo
Francisco fue elegido Papa en 2013 y falleció a los 88 años en abril de 2025.
Escribió el diario entre 1992 y 2024 y este fue editado por el cardenal argentino Víctor Manuel Fernández.
Según recoge AFP, Francisco le pidió ayuda a Fernández, prefecto del Dicasterio para la Doctrina de la Fe del Vaticano, para dar a conocer al mundo sus reflexiones.
Tras la muerte de Francisco, Fernández expresó su preocupación a su sucesor, León XIV, de que el libro "pudiera terminar abandonado en algún almacén".
Es así como finalmente recibió autorización para publicar algunos pasajes, señalando que "las preocupaciones espirituales presentes en su corazón son muy explícitas y pueden sernos de ayuda".
De acuerdo al medio británico The Guardian, el libro no contiene el diario completo ya que Francisco escribía sus pensamientos más personales en un código difícil de leer.

title: Sooryavanshi, 15, breaks sixes record by scoring 204 off 53 balls
rawText:
Sooryavanshi, 15, breaks sixes record by scoring 204 off 53 balls
- Published
India's 15-year-old batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hit the most sixes ever recorded in a senior men's innings in blazing 204 from 53 balls for India A against the United Arab Emirates.
While almost halving the record for the fastest double-century in List A cricket, Sooryavanshi hit 28 sixes and seven fours in the Asia Cup Rising Stars competition - easily breaking Chad Bowes' previous record of 103 balls from 2024.
The teenage opener also broke the record for the fastest century and 150, the latter of which he already held, before being caught at long-off with his side five runs from victory.
India A ultimately passed their target of 250, played against a UAE side that featured a number of internationals but was not their current first-choice side, in 14.2 overs in Doha.
Sooryavanshi now holds the following records in List A cricket, the categorisation given to senior one-day matches:
- Fastest fifty: 11 balls v Sri Lanka A, 21 June (previously Kaushalya Weeraratne, 12 balls, 1 November 2005)
- Fastest hundred: 28 balls, today (previously Jake Fraser-McGurk, 29 balls, 8 October 2023)
- Fastest 150: 40 balls, today (previously himself, 59 balls, 24 December 2025)
- Fastest 200: 52 balls, today (previously Chad Bowes, 103 balls, 22 October 2024)
The previous record for the most sixes in senior matches was 26, struck by Tanmay Agarwal in an innings of 366 for Hyderabad against Arunachal Pradesh in India's first-class Ranji Trophy competition in January 2024.
The record in List A cricket was 23 sixes, struck by D'Arcy Short for Queensland in his 257 against Tasmania on 28 September 2018.
Sooryavanshi also holds the records of being the youngest century-maker in both List A and T20 cricket and the youngest captain in T20s.
"The first thing that's required in this format is being fearless, he's got plenty of that," former India batter Deep Dasgupta told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"Technically he's quite unique. There is a tendency of being over-coached in this generation, there's so many coaches and when you start playing franchise cricket.
"The best part is he has been fast-tracked so he hasn't had a lot of coaches, he's kind of untouched. What you see of him is predominantly what his natural game is.
"That bat swing, the hand speed, which is very, very natural and one of the quickest you'll come across. Technically he's very gifted, he's very special and he's definitely the real deal."
Sooryavanshi has rapidly become a sensation in T20 cricket since making his debut in the Indian Premier League in 2025 at the age of 14.
He has hit two hundreds and six fifties in his first two seasons in the competition and has earned 10 caps for India in the shortest format since making his debut against England in July.
The left-hander, who was batting in only his 16th List A innings in Doha and made his second century in the format, is yet to play for India in 50-over cricket.
He put on partnerships of 68 with opening partner Abhishek Sharma, who scored 12, 40 with Prabhsimran Singh, who added just three, and 137 with Rinku Singh, who scored an unbeaten 27.
The India A side, which featured a number of internationals, restricted the UAE to 249-8 in 50 overs, external after their opposition had chosen to bat and swiftly reached 254-3 to win by seven wickets and guarantee their place in the semi-finals.
The Rising Stars competition features A sides from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan alongside squads from the UAE, Nepal and Hong Kong.
India A, who now top Group B, beat Nepal and lost to Pakistan A in their previous two matches in the competition, with Sooryavanshi making scores of 26 and 11.
Pakistan A will retake the top spot if they beat Nepal on Tuesday, with semi-finals on Thursday and Friday to follow before Sunday's final.

title: Iran vows to end U.S. naval blockade by "all available means"
rawText:
Live Updates: Iran says it will use all means to end U.S. blockade as Trump plays down escalating attacks
What to know about the Iran war today:
- The U.S. is investigating potential Iranian involvement in cyberattacks that targeted tankers carrying oil and other explosive substances, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.
- Iran said Monday it would use "all available means" to counter the U.S. naval blockade of the country's ports, which a foreign ministry official described as "an act of military aggression" against the country.
- President Trump said in a social media post Sunday that Iran had "launched more drones and missiles in the last week than at any time" during the nearly nine-month war, but that the increasing attacks had "done no damage."
U.S. reportedly investigating cyberattacks on oil tankers
The U.S. is investigating whether Iran is involved in cyberattacks targeting dozens of ships carrying oil and other explosive substances, according to sources familiar with the matter quoted by the Wall Street Journal.
As many as 50 ships carrying oil, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, the Journal reported, citing the sources. In some cases, ships have also received bomb threats.
According to the sources, Iran is the primary suspect of the incidents, while Russia is also seen as a possible culprit.
The Journal had previously reported two of the cyberattacks targeted ships heading to Texas in September.
Houthi media says 25 killed or missing after Saudi strikes
Houthi-affiliated news agency Saba said Tuesday that a Saudi strike on buses and trucks had left 25 people dead or missing in Yemen's southwest.
The Iran-backed fighters, who control swathes of Yemen, are battling a Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen's internationally recognised government.
"The toll from the Saudi enemy planes' targeting of buses and trucks in Wadi Mabaq, Lahj Governorate, has risen to 25 martyrs or missing, and six wounded," reported the Houthi-run Saba news agency, adding that the continued presence of Saudi aircraft over the area was hindering rescue efforts.
On Monday, the Houthi's military spokesperson Yahya Saree had reported the attack — without providing casualty figures — and vowed it would not go "unanswered."
Separate strikes on Monday killed 17 people and destroyed several buildings in the neighbouring coast province of Hodeida, the Houthis' telecommunications ministry said.
CBS/AFP
3 oil tankers struck naval mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran's navy says
The Iranian navy said in a statement carried on state media that three oil tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, resulting in "explosions and massive fires."
There were no immediate reports of casualties.
Iranian forces have been attacking shipping through the strait in a campaign aimed at hiking global energy prices to pressure the United States, which has imposed a crippling blockade on Iranian ports.
On Saturday, three other oil tankers were hit in what appeared to be the latest Iranian strikes on shipping through the strategic chokepoint.
CBS/AP
Top Iranian diplomat calls land blockade of Iran "impossible"
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called a land blockade of Iran "impossible" in comments shared Monday, according to Iranian state media. He also said pushing back against U.S. sanctions "is the duty of the entire country and its people," state media reported.
"The best way to counter this pressure is to make those imposing sanctions lose hope of achieving their goals, so they know this tool is ineffective and will remain so," Araghchi said.
Qatar's prime minister returns to Washington for Rubio meeting
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, in Washington, D.C., on Monday.

title: What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse
rawText:
What it's like at a climate conference as talks collapse
What it's like in the halls of a climate conference as it collapses
After two weeks of negotiations, international climate talks fail to reach an agreement. NPR's Rachel Waldholz was in Turkey for the conference.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:
International climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended today after negotiations fell apart. NPR's Rachel Waldholz has been at the conference and sent us this report.
RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: I'm here in the Antalya Expo Center, which, for the past two weeks, has been packed with some 70,000 people who came to the COP31 climate conference. Now it's almost completely empty. In fact, they're disassembling parts of the venue around me. The climate talks ran two days past their scheduled end. By the time the gavel fell, many negotiators had already left to catch their flights home. Australia climate chief Chris Bowen led the negotiations.
CHRIS BOWEN: I haven't slept for the last three nights, been negotiating all the way through, but more importantly, people on delegations came at it and gave it everything they had.
WALDHOLZ: Delegates came to Antalya with long wish lists, from electrifying more of the global economy to money for developing countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change. Looming over it all is that this is the first summit to squarely face the reality that the planet will miss a key target of the Paris Climate Agreement, reaching warming of 1.5 degrees Celsius or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above pre-Industrial levels. The U.N. says limiting that overshoot requires cutting the use of fossil fuels nearly in half in the next 10 to 15 years. Many countries wanted an agreement explicitly calling for a transition away from coal, oil and natural gas. But big oil-producing countries, like Saudi Arabia, blocked any mention of fossil fuels. Ultimately, the European Union decided no deal was better than the deal on the table. Darragh O'Brien is Ireland's environment minister.
DARRAGH O'BRIEN: We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.
WALDHOLZ: Many negotiators left the expo center dragging their suitcases on the way to the airport. They'll pick up negotiations next year at the next climate summit in Ethiopia. I'm Rachel Waldholz in Antalya, Turkey.

title: Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage
rawText:
All Delta flights in and out of Atlanta are facing significant delays on Sunday due to a problem with the system that calculates a plane’s weight and balance. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is Delta’s largest hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. While only Delta is impacted at the moment, disruptions at Hartsfield-Jackson could potentially affect other airports and airlines if delays continue to pile up.
Delta flights in and out of Atlanta delayed due to system outage
Major delays for Delta come just a week after a nationwide groundstop.
The issues with Delta’s systems in Atlanta come just one week after an FAA outage led to a nationwide groundstop and thousands of canceled flights. According to The New York Times:
The system that went offline calculates the total weight of an airplane, including its airframe, fuel, passengers and their baggage. The system also allows pilots to determine the plane’s center of gravity and whether the weight is evenly distributed — data points that help ensure safe passage.
“Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation,” the airline said in a statement on Sunday.

title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
rawText:
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

title: Hegseth alardea de la captura de Maduro en la primera visita a Venezuela de un secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. en décadas
rawText:
Hegseth alardea de la captura de Maduro en la primera visita a Venezuela de un secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. en décadas
  - Autor, Redacción
  - Título del autor, BBC News Mundo
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 3 min
"Hoy hace exactamente un año, el imputado fugitivo narcoterrorista Nicolás Maduro, el hombre que pasó más de una década entregándoles las fronteras y el territorio de Venezuela a terroristas de todas partes del mundo, se paró en un escenario no muy lejos de aquí y gritó en tono de burla: 'Vengan y agárrenme'. Bueno, nosotros respondimos a ese llamado".
Con esas palabras, el secretario de Defensa de EE.UU. Pete Hegseth, presumió de la captura de Maduro durante una visita a Venezuela en la que se reunió con la presidenta interina, Delcy Rodríguez, para firmar un acuerdo de cooperación militar.
Durante un discurso pronunciado en la sede de la Embajada de EE.UU. Hegseth describió la captura de Maduro como "la operación militar más sofisticada en la historia de América Latina" y aseguró que el 3 de enero -cuando fue ejecutada- pasará a la historia de Venezuela como "un día de liberación".
"Es un gran honor ser el primer secretario de Guerra en este siglo en pisar Venezuela. El peso de este momento no se me escapa. Hace apenas un año, mi presencia aquí, nuestra presencia aquí habría sido considerada imposible, casi inimaginable", dijo.
Hegseth afirmó que eso había sido posible gracias al mandatario estadounidense, Donald Trump.
"Tuvo el coraje para hacer lo que ningún presidente anterior estuvo dispuesto a hacer: defender la patria estadounidense con acciones, no solo con palabras. Y porque él lo hizo hace casi un año, los mejores y más valientes guerreros estadounidenses solucionaron un problema de 27 años de antigüedad para este hemisferio en cuestión de horas", apuntó.
"El resultado fue, como había predicho Maduro, 'no guerra, sí paz'. Paz a través de la fuerza para llevar a narcoterroristas hasta la justicia y empezar un nuevo capítulo para EE.UU., para Venezuela, para los militares venezolanos y para el hemisferio occidental", agregó luego.
Cooperación militar
La visita del jefe del Pentágono a Caracas se produjo en el contexto de una gira por países de América Latina.
Antes de su discurso en la sede diplomática, Hegseth acudió al Palacio de Miraflores, sede del Poder Ejecutivo, donde firmó con Delcy Rodríguez un acuerdo de cooperación militar entre el Pentágono y las Fuerzas Armadas de Venezuela.
El alto funcionario estadounidense dijo que se trata del "restablecimiento" de lazos militares entre ambos países.
Aunque no se ofrecieron muchos detalles, la prensa oficial en Venezuela aseguró que se trata de un acuerdo que "respetará la independencia y la soberanía nacional".
Hegseth calificó el pacto como "un restablecimiento de nuestra alianza de defensa" y afirmó que traía los saludos del presidente Trump, quien esperaba con interés trabajar juntos. "No solo en el ámbito militar contra los narcoterroristas y las organizaciones criminales", dijo, "sino también en el económico, aprovechando las extraordinarias capacidades de recursos de Venezuela".
Por su parte, Delcy Rodríguez elogió lo que describió como la "madurez política" que había permitido a estos dos antiguos enemigos reconstruir sus relaciones de trabajo. El acuerdo con el Pentágono "fortalecerá la capacidad de la Fuerza Armada Nacional Bolivariana", afirmó, al proporcionar "equipamiento operativo" y acceso a nuevas tecnologías.
El objetivo de este último acuerdo firmado con Washington, añadió, es "hacer frente a amenazas comunes".
Desde la captura de Maduro en enero, Estados Unidos asumió una suerte de tutela sobre Venezuela que incluye el control sobre la venta del petróleo de ese país. Además, respaldó la permanencia de Delcy Rodríguez en el poder como presidenta interina.

title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
rawText:
A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
rawText:
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
